name: Elephant Gambit
summary: The Elephant Gambit (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5), an offbeat countergambit where Black gambits a pawn to strike the centre and seek quick development.
intro: The Elephant Gambit arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5, when Black immediately counterattacks in the centre rather than defending the e5-pawn. It is an offbeat, provocative gambit: after 3.exd5 e4 Black offers a pawn to gain time by hitting the f3-knight and opening lines for rapid development. Objectively the gambit is dubious, since White can keep an edge with accurate play, but it remains a dangerous surprise weapon against unprepared opponents. Black stakes everything on quick piece activity and initiative, while White aims to consolidate the extra material and return it only for a lasting positional advantage.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 d5 exd5 e4 Qe2 Nf6 d3 Qxd5 Nbd2

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: Black's whole idea is speed and disruption. By meeting 2.Nf3 with 2...d5, Black refuses to sit passively and instead tries to seize the initiative. After 3.exd5 e4 the advanced e4-pawn cramps White and attacks the f3-knight, forcing it to move or be defended awkwardly. Black wants to recapture on d5 with the queen, develop the pieces quickly toward White's king, and exploit any hesitation. The gambit thrives on surprise and tactical alertness: if White drifts into a passive setup, Black's lead in development and open lines can generate a strong, lasting attack.

White's task is to prove the gambit unsound by careful, greedy defence. Accepting the pawn and refusing to panic is key: 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2 pins the advanced e4-pawn and targets it, while the simple 3.Nxe5 is also strong and keeps material. White develops solidly, often with d3 to undermine the e4-pawn, Nbd2 to reroute the knight, and quick castling. The extra pawn and sounder structure give White the pull; the winning plan is to blunt Black's initiative, exchange active pieces, and convert either the material or the resulting positional edge in a calmer middlegame.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The critical main line runs 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2, immediately hitting the e4-pawn and daring Black to defend it. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 Qxd5 6.Nbd2, White chips away at the centre and prepares to complete development while keeping the extra pawn or an improved structure. Black regains the d5-pawn with the queen but must reckon with White's smooth mobilisation. This is the tabiya where theory considers White better with precise play, though the positions stay concrete and it is easy for an unfamiliar defender to go wrong.

The other principled reply is 3.Nxe5, when White simply captures the pawn and challenges Black to prove compensation. Black usually continues 3...Bd6, attacking the e5-knight, or 3...dxe4, opening the position; both lead to sharp, concrete play. White does well to develop naturally, return the extra pawn if needed, and steer toward a solid structure. Practically, many Elephant Gambit games are decided by preparation: the defender who knows the critical 4.Qe2 and 3.Nxe5 lines usually emerges with a pleasant, risk-free advantage, while an unprepared opponent can quickly drift into trouble.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Elephant Gambit is one of the oldest documented replies to 2.Nf3, analysed as far back as the 17th and 18th centuries and appearing in early opening manuals. It has carried several names, including the Queen's Pawn Countergambit and, more colourfully, the Elephant Gambit. Never a mainstream weapon at the highest level, it has survived as a favourite of gambiteers and correspondence players who enjoy sharp, unbalanced positions. Modern engines confirm that White should hold an edge, so today it lives mainly as a surprise weapon in rapid and blitz, where its tricks retain real practical bite.
